# Research Question and Background 

## Research Question
Do census tracts with more waste sites tend to have worse health outcomes?
## Background 
Environmental justice in the United States has long been connected to waste management and the siting of waste facilities. One of the earliest events that helped spark the environmental justice movement occurred in Warren County, North Carolina in the 1980s, when residents protested the dumping of polychlorinated biphenyls (PCBs) in a nearby hazardous waste landfill (Rector, 2018). Since then, the location of waste facilities has remained a concern in environmental justice discussions and research. These concerns are still relevant today, including in California, where waste production continues to increase and communities often question the impacts of living near waste sites.

Solid waste is defined as “all solid or semi-solid waste… mostly includ[ing] domestic or household waste" (Siddiqua et al., 2022, p.58518). Placing waste sites near residential areas can create environmental risks such as methane accumulation, groundwater contamination, and property damage (Siddiqua et al., 2022). Waste facilities can also generate pollutants that affect nearby communities. When organic materials like food waste decompose in landfills, they produce byproducts such as leachate and landfill gas (Chen et al., 2021). Leachate forms when rainwater mixes with decomposing waste and can contain contaminants such as ammonia and microbes (ACTenviro, 2025). If not properly contained, this liquid can seep into surrounding soil or groundwater.

Landfill decomposition also produces landfill gas. Because landfills are mostly anaerobic environments, microorganisms break down organic waste and release methane and carbon dioxide. Methane contributes to greenhouse gas emissions and can also lead to the formation of tropospheric ozone, which is known to aggravate lung diseases and may contribute to asthma development (EPA, 2025b). In addition, landfill emissions can produce strong odors that affect nearby residents. For example, some landfill facilities in Los Angeles have generated thousands of odor complaints from surrounding communities (South Coast AQMD, 2025). Although some studies have found links between waste facilities and health impacts (Siddiqua et al., 2022), many focus on individual sites rather than broader regional patterns. Fewer studies look at the spatial relationship between waste facility locations and population health indicators across larger areas in California. This project examines that relationship by exploring whether communities located closer to waste facilities experience worse health outcomes.


# Materials and Methods 
Here is a brief overview of my exploratory data analysis process, beginning with data selection.

## Datasets Used 

**Health Data**

To ensure spatial consistency across datasets, this analysis focuses on health indicators available at the census tract level. Many health datasets are only available at the county level, which makes them difficult to integrate with tract-level environmental data. As a result, several potential indicators were excluded from the analysis. For example, birth-related indicators such as preterm births and birthweight were not included because tract-level data were not available for the same time period.

The health indicators used in this study come from CDC PLACES and were accessed through PolicyMap. For more information about PolicyMap, go here: [https://unl.libguides.com/policymap]. 

The following health indicators were selected:
Asthma: Estimated prevalence of current asthma among adults aged 18 or older in 2023 (crude percent). Source: CDC PLACES
Cancer: Estimated prevalence of cancer (excluding skin cancer) among adults aged 18 or older in 2023. Source: CDC PLACES
Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Disease (COPD): Estimated prevalence of COPD among adults aged 18 or older in 2023 (crude percent). Source: CDC PLACES


**Waste Site and Facility Data**
Waste site location data were obtained from the CalRecycle Solid Waste Information System (SWIS) database.

I only filtered out an extreme outlier site and facilities categorized as planned. I chose to keep both active and closed waste facilities because I was interested in historical land use and how past waste management activities might still affect surrounding communities. Even if a site is no longer active, previous waste handling practices may have left lasting environmental impacts. By including these sites, the analysis aims to capture a broader picture of how both current and historical waste infrastructure may relate to present-day health outcomes.

**Demographic Data** 
Demographic variables were obtained using the tidycensus API, which provides access to U.S. Census Bureau data within R. This analysis uses the American Community Survey (ACS) 5-year estimates, which are the standard for census tract–level analysis. The ACS 1-year estimates were not used because they are not available for census tracts.

# Exploratory Data Analysis
This exploratory data analysis explores the relationship between waste sites and prevalence of health issues. It begins by cleaning and joining the data sets. Then it analyzes the linear relationships between variables. Finally, it runs regressions and analyzes the significance of associated relationships.

## Data Wrangling

### Examine data 

**re-examine source data** 

Any datasets extracted using PolicyMap come with a metadata file. CalRecycle's dataset does not. Examine all metadata files and CalRecycle's website. Take notes on differences, definitions, etc.

- CDC_Places_Asthma.csv
  - p_crd_casthma represents "Estimated prevalence of current asthma among adults aged 18 or older in 2023."

- CDC_Places_Cancer.csv 
  - p_crd_cancer represents "Estimated prevalence of cancer (excluding skin cancer) among adults aged 18 or older in 2023."
  
- CDC_Places_COPD.csv 
  - p_crd_copd represents "Estimated prevalence of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease among adults aged 18 or older in 2023."
  
- Site.csv 
  - Metadata avaliable here: [https://www.arcgis.com/home/item.html?id=f96a4878acf644d4923756bcf2ec90cb]. 
  - Geography in longitude/latitude format 
  - No GEOID
- Census data 
  - Compatible with CDC_Places
  
In order to match SWIS point data to demographic+ health data, a spatial join is needed. 


```{r}
# load the dplyr package, which hosts the useful glimpse() function
library(dplyr)
```

preview data using the glimpse() function or View(). 

All health indicator data sets will have the same columns + their respective health indicator column. The SWIS data looks a little bit different, with various unique variables-- some of which are not needed. Like the ca data, this set contains a "NAME" column, but it represents the sites name rather than the Census tract name. 

```{r}
# waste site and facility data 
glimpse(sites)
```

summary stats, outliers, NA's 
```{r}
summary(ca)

## The age columns contain NA values. 
```


All Census data and CDC_Places data is tract level. The site dataset is a little bit more complicated, offering point data through two longitude and latitude columns. 
  - Census: 2023
  - CRD_Places: 2023 
  - CalRecycle: Copyrighted 2026, no way to know when sites were added. However, the Site.Operational.Status column lists sites that are planning, meaning that they yet begun operations and cannot currently accept waste. I will be removing these sites out of the dataset. 
  
  

### Clean Data Sets + Merge 

```{r}
# Asthma, Cancer, COPD, PM25, and ca all share Census GEOID (Geographic identifier) columns.

# Use select() function from dplyr package to select needed columns from each health dataset. In this case, only keep the "GeoID" and the health indicator columns in each set. Rename "GeoID" columns to "GEOID". Convert health variables to numeric, rather that character (for future plotting).

Asthma_C <- Asthma %>%
  select(GeoID, p_crd_casthma) %>%
  rename(GEOID = GeoID, Asthma = p_crd_casthma) %>%
  mutate(Asthma = as.numeric(Asthma))

Cancer_C <- Cancer %>%
  select(GeoID, p_crd_cancer) %>%
  rename(GEOID = GeoID,Cancer = p_crd_cancer)%>%
  mutate(Cancer = as.numeric(Cancer))

COPD_C <- COPD %>% 
  select(GeoID, p_crd_copd) %>%
  rename(GEOID = GeoID, COPD = p_crd_copd) %>%
  mutate(COPD = as.numeric(COPD))


# When converting the health indicators to numeric, the following warning appears: "NAS introduced by coercion". The following code uses the unique() function on the original Asthma data to see what values appear in the p_crd_casthma column-- removing duplicates. 

unique(Asthma$p_crd_casthma)

## Previously, I used sum(is.na(data$column)) to identify missing values. However, this function doesn't look for text such as N/A. Converting to numeric doesn't actually introduce new NA values. It's just forcing the "N/A" strings to convert into real NA values. 

```

```{r}
# Clean California demographic data 
ca <- ca %>%
  mutate(pct_white = 100 * whiteE / tpoprE, # convert estimates into percentages
         pct_black = 100 * blkE / tpoprE,
         pct_asian = 100 * asianE / tpoprE,
         pct_hisp = 100 * hispE / tpoprE) %>%
  select(GEOID, NAME, tpoprE, ageE, pct_white, pct_black, pct_asian, pct_hisp) %>% # kept, GEOID, NAME, total population, and percentages
  rename(Tract_Name = NAME) #rename NAME to Tract_Name
  
```

```{r}
# Merge the following: Asthma_C, Cancer_C, COPD_C, PM25_C, ca. Use the "GEOID" column as the key.
indicator_dem_data <- Asthma_C %>%
  select(GEOID, Asthma) %>%
  left_join(Cancer_C %>% 
              select(GEOID, Cancer), by="GEOID") %>%
  left_join(COPD_C %>%
              select(GEOID, COPD), by="GEOID") %>%
  left_join(ca %>%
              select(GEOID, Tract_Name, tpoprE, ageE, pct_white, pct_black, pct_asian, pct_hisp), by="GEOID")
```


```{r}
# clean waste site data. 

## keep columns that help locate the site spatially, identify the site, determine sites status (to clean out planned sites), type of waste facility 

sites_C <- sites %>%
  filter(Site.Operational.Status != "Planned") %>%
  select(SWIS.Number, # unique site identifier 
         Name, # site name, need to rename
         Latitude, # coordinates
         Longitude,
         Site.Operational.Status, # operational status: closed, opened , planned. Will need to exclude planned sites from the analysis, because they have not yet begun accepting waste or may not even exist.
         Site.Regulatory.Status, # regulatory status: permitted, permitted, etc. 
         ClosedIllegalAbandonedCategory, # waste category, may be useful for classifying sites by risk sites or exploring questions like "Do sites correlated with X variable tend to be abandoned?" 
         County # will be cool to explore
         )%>%
  rename(Site.Name = Name)

```

```{r}
# Remove df that are no longer need, just to keep environment clean

rm(Asthma, Asthma_C, Cancer, Cancer_C, ca, COPD, COPD_C, sites, v23)

# now I am left with two clean datasets: indicator_dem_data & sites_C
```

### Spatial Join
indicator_dem_data uses GEOID to match data to census tracts. sites_C uses coordinates. A spatial join is needed in order to determine which sites fall in which census tracts. Ultimately, the goal is to calculate the number of sites per tract. 



Since I am working with vector data, I am going to use the sf package. Learn more about it here: [https://r-spatial.github.io/sf/]. 

```{r}
library(sf)
```
convert data frames into spatial objects
```{r}
# convert sites to spatial points using the st_as_sf() function, which will turn the standard data frame sites_C into a spatial object. 

sites_sf <- st_as_sf(sites_C, 
                     coords = c("Longitude", "Latitude"),
                     crs = 4326 #CalRecycle never specifies what CRS they use. Assume they are using WGS84 
                     )
```

```{r}
# obtain geometry for indicator_dem_data, which is currently listed as a tbl/ data.frame, meaning there is no spatial geometry. 
class(indicator_dem_data)

```

In order to add geometry, the tigris package is needed. tigirs allows users to access U.S. Census Bureau geography shapefiles. Learn more about it here: [https://www.rdocumentation.org/packages/tigris/versions/2.2.1]

```{r}
library(tigris)
```
obtain tract geometry 
```{r}
# Get census tract boundaries using tigris function tracts() 
tracts <- tracts(state = "CA", 
                 year = 2022)

# tract GeoId's are matched to polygons
glimpse(tracts)
```

```{r}
# Join indicator_dem_data to tracts
tracts_sf <- tracts %>%
  select(GEOID, geometry) %>%
  left_join(indicator_dem_data, by = "GEOID")

# clean environment 
rm(tracts, sites_C, indicator_dem_data)
```

```{r}
# Align coordinate systems 

## check CRS 
st_crs(sites_sf)

st_crs(tracts_sf)

## different CRS, need to match sites_sf to tracts_sf
sites_sf <- st_transform(sites_sf, st_crs(tracts_sf))
```
Conduct a spatial join to find the number of sites per tract 
```{r}

## Spatial object will contain all health waste site data in one. There will be multiple rows per census tracts. 
## NOTE: sites_sf geometry is made of points. tracts_sf is made of polygons. The following code matches points to the polygons that contain them. 

sites_with_tract <- st_join(sites_sf, tracts_sf)
```

```{r}
# number of sites per tract 

site_counts <- sites_with_tract %>%
  st_drop_geometry()%>% #not needed
  group_by(GEOID) %>%
  summarise(waste_sites = n()) 

# every census tract is now matched to a # of waste sites. 
glimpse(site_counts)
```

```{r}
# join site counts into tracts_sf, which will be the primary data anlaysis set 

tracts_sf <- tracts_sf %>%
  left_join(site_counts, by="GEOID")
```

```{r}
# results 
glimpse(tracts_sf)

``` 

```{r}
# many rows have NA values under waste_sites.
summary(tracts_sf) # The minimum is listed as 1 under waste_sites column-- meaning that rows with NA values represent tracts with 0 waste sites. 

# Note that there other columns contain NA values as well. Together, NA values represent less than 1% of data. 

```

```{r}
library(tidyr) ##offers the replace_na() function

# you can also replace NA values using base R. 
```

```{r}
# clean tracts_sf, and create logarithmic site group categories
tracts_sf <- tracts_sf %>%
  mutate(waste_sites = replace_na(waste_sites, 0), # NA's here represent 0 waste sites
         waste_sites = as.numeric(waste_sites), # waste_sites should be numeric
         site_group = floor(log2(waste_sites+1))) # group # of waste sites in log bins

```

```{r}
# view site group bins 
tracts_sf %>%
  st_drop_geometry() %>%
  group_by(site_group) %>%
  summarise(min_sites = min(waste_sites),
            max_sites = max(waste_sites),
            n_tracts = n())

# based on the log bins, create labels 

tracts_sf <- tracts_sf %>%
  mutate(site_group_label = case_when(site_group == 0 ~ "0",
                                      site_group == 1 ~ "1-2",
                                      site_group == 2 ~ "3-6",
                                      site_group == 3 ~ "7-14",
                                      site_group == 4 ~ "15-30",
                                      site_group >= 5 ~ "31+"))

summary(tracts_sf) # Note that there other columns contain NA values as well. Together, NA values represent less than 1% of data.
```





```{r}
# create cleaned analysis dataset for statistical analysis
tracts_sf_clean <- tracts_sf %>%
  drop_na(Asthma, COPD, ageE, pct_white, pct_black, pct_asian, pct_hisp) %>% #remove tracts with missing values on key analysis variables 
  filter(tpoprE > 0) # only include tracts where the population is above 0. 

```


## Data Analysis 

My primary research question is: Do tracts with more waste sites experience worse health outcomes or higher pollution exposure? 


### Examine variable distribution
The analysis will begin by examining variables and their distributions. With over 9000 census tracts, plots need to handle large N well, show skew + outliers, and be easy to interpret. 

**Descriptive Statistics** 
Summarize key variables from tracts_sf_clean to see central tendency, skew, and variability. 

  For exposure, examine waste_sites and log_waste_sites. 
  For health outcomes, examine asthma, COPD, Cancer 
  For demographics, examine ageE, pct_white, pct_asian, pct_hisp. 
  
Load the flextable package, which helps make neat tables. For more information, please refer to : [https://epirhandbook.com/en/new_pages/tables_presentation.html]

```{r}
library(flextable)
```
create statistics tables

```{r}
#prepare df for a summary statistics table 
summary_table <- tracts_sf_clean %>%
  st_drop_geometry() %>% # geometry not needed 
  select(waste_sites, Asthma, COPD, Cancer, ageE, pct_white, pct_black, pct_asian, pct_hisp)

# group variables, and take the summary statistics
summary_table <- summary_table %>%
  pivot_longer(everything(), names_to = "Variable", values_to = "Value") %>%
  group_by(Variable) %>%
  summarise(Mean = mean(Value, na.rm = TRUE), 
            Median = median(Value, na.rm = TRUE),
            SD = sd(Value, na.rm = TRUE),
            IQR = IQR(Value, na.rm = TRUE)) %>%
  mutate(across(c(Mean, Median, SD, IQR), round, 2)) %>%
  mutate(Variable = recode(Variable,
                     waste_sites = "Waste Sites",
                     Asthma = "Asthma Prevanlence (%) ",
                     COPD = "COPD Prevalence (%)",
                     Cancer = "Cancer Prevalence (%)",
                     ageE = "Median Age",
                     pct_white = "% White",
                     pct_black = "% Black",
                     pct_asian = "% Asian",
                     pct_hisp = "% Hispanic"))

# final table
flextable(summary_table) %>%
  autofit() %>%
  align(align = "center", part = "all") %>%
  theme_apa()

```
Based on the table, there are a few takeaways. Waste facility counts are right-skewed, with most tracts having no sites and a small number having multiple facilities. Asthma, COPD, and cancer prevalence appears relatively evenly distributed across census tracts, but there is a slight right skew since the mean is highly higher than the median. 

**Waste Facility Distribution**
This section explores how common waste sites are across census tracts. 

Create a table showing the frequency of waste facilities. It should contain the following columns: Waste Site Category, Number of Tracts, Percent 

```{r}
# frequency table 
waste_distribution <- tracts_sf_clean %>%
  st_drop_geometry() %>%
  mutate(site_group_label = factor(site_group_label, 
                                   levels = c("0", "1-2", "3-6", "7-14", "15-30", "31+"))) %>%
  count(site_group_label) %>%
  mutate(percent = round(100 * n / sum(n), 2)) %>%
  rename("Waste Site Category" = site_group_label,
         "Number of Tracts" = n,
         "Percent of Tracts" = percent)

flextable(waste_distribution) %>%
  autofit() %>%
  align(align = "center", part = "all") %>%
  theme_apa()
```


Create a histogram for waste_sites to show skew

  Load in ggplot2, a package designed to visualize data. Learn more here:
  [https://r-graph-gallery.com/ggplot2-package.html]

```{r}
library(ggplot2)
```

```{r}
# make plot 
waste_skew0 <- ggplot(tracts_sf_clean, aes(x = waste_sites)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 1, fill = "red", color = "white") +
  labs(title = "Distribution of Waste Sites per Census Tract",
       x = "Number of Waste Sites",
       y = "Number of Census Tracts") +

waste_skew0
```


**Investigate outliers**

This section investigates tracts with extremely high waste site counts. It specifically focuses on the tract with 120 waste sites. 

First, identify the tract with the greatest number of waste sites. 

```{r}
# isolate greatest values 
tracts_sf_clean %>%
  st_drop_geometry %>%
  arrange(desc(waste_sites))%>%
  select(GEOID, Tract_Name, waste_sites) %>%
  head(10)
```
```{r}
# look at sites inside the tract with 120 sites

sites_with_tract %>%
  filter(GEOID == "06037207305") # filter for site, see first 10 features

View(sites_with_tract %>% filter(GEOID == "06037207305")) # view all the sites
```

I can see that sites are not repeats and may actually exist. I have two suspicions. First, this is a large tract located in the hilly region of the San Fernando Valley/ Los Angeles County. Second, many sites are closed because they are either smaller historical dump sites (pre-1990s) before regulations tightened on landfills. 


```{r}
# Map the outlier tract. 
outlier_tract <- tracts_sf_clean %>%
  filter(GEOID == "06037207305")

ggplot() +
  geom_sf(data = tracts_sf_clean, fill = "grey95", color = "black") +
  geom_sf(data = outlier_tract, fill = "red", color = "red", size = 1) +
  coord_sf(xlim = c(-119, -117), ylim = c(33.5, 35)) +
  labs(title = "Location of High Waste Site Tract in Los Angeles County") +
  theme_minimal()
```
It looks like the tract is located somewhere in a dense region of Los Angeles. Perhaps records represent historical waste sites, which have been developed over or these are multiple records for the same facility under different names. 

```{r}
# Check if many sites have the same coordinates. 
sites_with_tract %>%
  filter(GEOID == "06037207305") %>%
  count(geometry, sort = TRUE)

# all 120 sites have the same point location, meaning that these are duplicates or historical records. 
```

Based on the output above, 120 sites are stacked at a single coordinate. Several explanations are possible. First, the dataset may contain multiple regulatory records for a single facility, though this seems unlikely. Second, some records may represent different historic sites that were later aggregated under one location, which appears more plausible. Examining the rows within the GEOID reveals variation in the Site.Name field. Some site names reference street locations—for example, “Bradley Avenue Dump.” Other names repeat institutional owners such as “City of LA Department of Public Works.” A likely explanation is that these records correspond to smaller historic dumping sites that operated before modern regulatory systems were established. In several cases, ownership is listed as unknown, suggesting that some records may have been digitized from incomplete historical documentation or that the sites operated informally. The shared coordinate likely reflects older data-keeping practices in which facilities were assigned a generic location, such as a city centroid or approximate reference point. To investigate further, I examine the census tract associated with these records

The U.S. Census Bureau provides a useful Maps tool that allows users to filter geographic entities such as census tracts: [https://data.census.gov/map?layer=VT_2022_040_00_PP_D1&loc=43.3751,-113.1138,z1.4027]. 

The sites_with_tract object includes a Tract_Name column, which can be used to locate the tract within the Census Bureau map interface. In the tool, select View Filters → Geographies → Census Tract → California → Los Angeles County, then paste the tract name into the search bar and toggle on the matching tract.

```{r}
# view tract name 
outlier_tract$Tract_Name
```

```{r}
# Here is a screenshot of Census Tract 2075.05  U.S. Census Bureau Maps Website, which is highlighted in light blue. 
knitr::include_graphics("Census_Tract_2073_05_Los Angeles County_California.png")
```

The tract is located in downtown Los Angeles and represents a dense urban mixed-use area.

To further investigate why so many sites appear stacked at a single coordinate, I searched site names and street names using Google Maps. Although these searches could be performed in R using a Google Maps API (e.g., with the ggmap package), Google charges for API requests. Instead, I conducted the searches using the Google Maps mobile application.For reproducibility, I include the Plus Codes associated with each location and screenshots of the map results. Plus Codes are searchable location identifiers, similar to street addresses, that allow users to return to specific map locations even if they lack a formal address.After searching Google Maps, it becomes clear that street names within the census tract do not match some of the street names referenced in the site records. For example, there is no Bradley Avenue within this tract. However, Google Maps identifies two streets named Bradley Avenue elsewhere in Los Angeles.

  
      
```{r}
# Plus Code: 85637HV3+RP 
## Specifically appears under the search result for : "Bradley Avenue Los Angeles, CA". It goes into the Slymar and Pacoima neighborhoods of the LA San Fernando Region. 

# Display Google Maps Screenshot

knitr::include_graphics("85637HV3_plus_RP.PNG")
```

```{r}

## Specifically appears under the search : "Bradley Avenue Sun Valley, CA". Sun Valley is a neighborhood located in the San Fernando valley region of LA. 

# Display Google Maps Screenshot
knitr::include_graphics("85636JHF_plus_HW.PNG")
```
Viewing these two locations on the map shows that the streets run in the same general direction and are located near one another. They are separated by several industrial facilities, including waste-related operations such as the Angeles C & D Public Dump. The street segments appear as though they may once have been connected before later development divided them. 

Various other site names refer to streets that do not exist within the census tract but exist within the City of Los Angeles. 

This pattern suggests that the coordinate associated with the stacked records likely represents a generic reference point used in older data-keeping practices rather than the true locations of the sites. The coordinate may have been assigned as a placeholder when precise geographic coordinates were unavailable. As a result, multiple historic records appear stacked at the same coordinate even though the actual dumping sites were likely located elsewhere.

Going forward, I am operating the the assumption that the coordinate is a place holder location and the points do not represent real spatial positions. Including these points in a spatial analysis artificially inflates waste site counts. A small number of additional tracts contain between 31 and 40 facilites, which may also reflect stacked coordinates, though time constraints prevents further investigation. 

Rather than verifying if these all tracts contain stacked points, I am going to look at tract with the 2nd highest number of waste sites and make a decision on how to analyze my data going forward. 

```{r}
# isolate greatest values again
tracts_sf_clean %>%
  st_drop_geometry %>%
  arrange(desc(waste_sites))%>%
  select(GEOID, Tract_Name, waste_sites) %>%
  head(10)
```


```{r}
# investigate tract with the second highest number of sites: 06029003304

sites_with_tract%>%
  filter(GEOID == "06029003304") # filter for site, see first 10 features
     
```

```{r}
# Check if many sites have the same coordinates for tract 06029003304
sites_with_tract %>%
  filter(GEOID == "06029003304") %>%
  count(geometry, sort = TRUE)

# view rows sharing this GEOID
View(sites_with_tract %>% filter(GEOID == "06029003304")) 

```
The tract with the second-highest facility count (38 records)-Census Tract 33.04; Kern County; California- contains 10 unique coordinates, indicating that the records may reflect multiple facility locations rather than a single placeholder coordinate. Some site names are similar (e.g., facilities labeled “North” or “South”), suggesting related operations within the same area. However, it is possible that some coordinates represent approximate or placeholder locations and may fall slightly outside the tract boundary. The records still exhibit meaningful spatial distribution because facilities include active sites and multiple unique coordinates. Because of this, the tract and any other tracts with less waste sites will be retained in the analysis. 


**exclude extreme outlier**
Census Tract 2073.05 in Los Angeles County; California contains 120 waste facility records located at one identical coordinate, indicating a placeholder location used in historical data records. This tract represents an extreme anomoly compared to the rest of the dataset. 

Although other tracts may contain stacked records, they still include multiple distinct coordinates suggesting some meaningful spatial distribution. Contrastingly, the Census Tract 2073.05 has one coordinate for 120 records. Including this tract would skew distribution of waste sites and distort visualizations such as histograms and scatterplots. Additionally Census Tract 2073.05 would bias statistical analysis by assigning an artificially high number of facilities to a tract where the sites may not actually be located, potentially weakening the relationship between waste site counts and health indicators. To prevent this tract from distorting the analysis, it will be excluded from tract-level calculations. All other tracts are retained. 

```{r}
# exclude Census Tract 2073.05 in Los Angeles County; California 
tracts_analysis <- tracts_sf_clean %>% 
  filter(GEOID!="06037207305")
```


**reexamaine waste site distribution ** 
Remake the plot of waste site distribution
```{r}
# make plot 
ggplot(tracts_analysis, aes(x = waste_sites)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 1, fill = "red", color = "white") +
  labs(title = "Distribution of Waste Sites per Census Tract",
       x = "Number of Waste Sites",
       y = "Number of Census Tracts") +
  theme_minimal()
```
Remake the table 
```{r}
waste_distribution <- tracts_analysis %>%
  st_drop_geometry() %>%
  mutate(site_group_label = factor(site_group_label, 
                                   levels = c("0", "1-2", "3-6", "7-14", "15-30", "31+"))) %>%
  count(site_group_label) %>%
  mutate(percent = round(100 * n / sum(n), 2)) %>%
  rename("Waste Site Category" = site_group_label,
         "Number of Tracts" = n,
         "Percent of Tracts" = percent)

flextable(waste_distribution) %>%
  autofit() %>%
  align(align = "center", part = "all") %>%
  theme_apa()

```

**correlation matrix**  
Explore the numeric relationships using a correlation matrix. 



```{r}
# Revise tracts_analysis
glimpse(tracts_analysis)
```

```{r}
# the tibble package contains the rownames_to_column() function, which allows users to move the row names into a column before making a table. 

# open package()
library(tibble)
``` 

```{r}
# prep data for correlation matrix

cor_data <- tracts_analysis %>%
  st_drop_geometry() %>%
  select(Asthma, Cancer, COPD, ageE, pct_white, pct_black, pct_asian, pct_hisp, waste_sites) 

```

```{r}
# create matrix
cor_matrix <- cor(cor_data, use = "complete.obs", method = "pearson") %>%
  as.data.frame() %>%
  rownames_to_column("Variable")

cor_matrix

```

```{r}
# visualize correlation matrix using ggplot geom_tile() function. It is also possible to do in base R() with heatmap() or using the "ggcorrplot" package, which is designed to visualize correlation matrices. 

## convert to matrix to long format (for it to work in ggplot)

cor_long <- cor_matrix %>%
  rename(Var1 = Variable) %>%
  pivot_longer(-Var1, names_to = "Var2", values_to = "correlation") %>%
  mutate(Var1 = recode(Var1,
                       ageE = "Median Age",
                       pct_white = "White (%)",
                       pct_black = "Black (%)",
                       pct_asian = "Asian (%)",
                       pct_hisp = "Hispanic (%)",
                       waste_sites = "Waste Sites"),
         Var2 = recode(Var2, 
                       ageE = "Median Age",
                       pct_white = "White (%)",
                       pct_black = "Black (%)",
                       pct_asian = "Asian (%)",
                       pct_hisp = "Hispanic (%)",
                       waste_sites = "Waste Sites"))
## view results 
cor_long
```

```{r}

# ggplot orders axes alphabetically. To control the order that my variables appear in, I am creating a vector specifying the order I want. 
var_order <- c( "Waste Sites","Asthma","COPD","Cancer","Median Age","White (%)", "Black (%)", "Asian (%)","Hispanic (%)")

# apply variable order to cor_long 
cor_long <- cor_long %>%
  mutate( 
    Var1 = factor(Var1, levels = var_order),
    Var2 = factor(Var2, levels = var_order))


# use ggplot to visualize the matrix w colors 
Pearson_Matrix <- ggplot(cor_long, aes(Var1, Var2, fill = correlation)) +
  geom_tile(color = "black") + # draw borders between tiles
  geom_text(aes(label = round(correlation, 2)), size = 3) + 
  scale_fill_gradient2(low = "#2166AC", # strong negative correlations
                       mid = "white", # zero correlation
                       high = "#B2182B", # strong positive correlation
                       midpoint = 0, #w where neutral colors happen
                       limits = c(-1, 1)) + # full correlatino range
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1)) + # stop labels from overlapping 
  labs(title = "Correlation Matrix of Health, Demographic, and Waste Site Variables", 
       x = "", # Removing x-axis label
       y = "", # Removing y-axis label
       fill = "Pearson r")


# References 
## [https://r-graph-gallery.com/79-levelplot-with-ggplot2.html]

Pearson_Matrix

```
Looking at the correlation matrix above, correlations between waste sites and all other variables appear rather weak. There is a very slight positive correlation between the health variables and the number of waste sites present, with COPD being the highest. 

#### Regressions
Test whether waste sites predict health outcomes, controlling for demographics

Run regressions
```{r}
# Asthma 
model_asthma <- lm(Asthma ~ waste_sites + pct_white + pct_black + pct_asian + pct_hisp + ageE, 
                   data = tracts_analysis)
model_asthma
```

```{r}
# COPD
model_copd <- lm(COPD ~ waste_sites + pct_white + pct_black + pct_asian + pct_hisp + ageE, 
                 data = tracts_analysis)

model_copd
```
Holding demographic composition and median age constant, each additional waste site is associated with a 0.15 percentage point increase in COPD prevalence. However, demographic and age variables appear to have stronger relationships with COPD rates than waste site density.

```{r}
# Cancer 
model_cancer <- lm(Cancer ~ waste_sites + pct_white + pct_black + pct_asian + pct_hisp + ageE, 
                   data = tracts_analysis)

model_cancer

```
To better understand the regression results, create a coefficient dot-whisker plot. To do so, I am referring to the this GitHub page: [https://felixhaass.github.io/dataviz_ggplot2/session4.html]

```{r}
# load packages
library("dotwhisker")
library("gapminder")
```

```{r}
# use dwplot() to select regression models 
regression_plot <- dwplot(list(Asthma = model_asthma, Cancer = model_cancer, COPD = model_copd)) + 
  #set colors for the health variables 
  scale_color_manual(values = c("Asthma" = "dodgerblue2", "Cancer" = "deeppink","COPD" = "forestgreen" )) +
  # draw a horizontal line for easier visual interpretation
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", color = "black") +
  scale_y_discrete(limits = c("waste_sites", "pct_white", "pct_black", "pct_asian", "pct_hisp", "ageE"),
                   labels = c(waste_sites = "Waste Sites", pct_white = "% White", pct_black = "% Black", pct_asian = "% Asian", pct_hisp = "% Hispanic", ageE = "Median Age" ) ) +
  labs(title = "Regression Estimates for Predictors of Asthma, Cancer, and COPD Prevalence (%)",
       x = "Coefficient Estimate",
       y = "",
       color = NULL) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(legend.position = "top", panel.grid.minor = element_blank(), axis.text.y = element_text(size = 11), plot.title = element_text(face = "bold")
  )

# results 
regression_plot
```
If the coefficient point is 0, then there is no relationship between predictor and the health outcome. Any points to the right of the dashed line indicate a positive relationship. Any points to the left of the dashed line indicate a negative relationship. The lines surroinding the coefficient represent confidence intervals. 

COPD shows the strongest relationship with waste sites, as the coefficient is positive and located far to the right of 0. This means that census tracts with more waste facilities tend to have a higher COPD prevalence. The confidence interval is fully on the positive side. 

Asthma shows a positive relationship, with the coefficient being slightly to the right of 0. This suggests that more waste sites are associated slightly higher asthma prevalence. The relationship is much smaller than COPD. 

Cancer appears negative and near 0. This suggests a very weak negative relationship. 


*significance*
Here, I am looking to see whether the associations between waste site counts and the health outcomes are considered statistically signficant. If the p value is les than 0.05, then the relationship is statisically signficant. 

```{r}
# Asthma 
summary(model_asthma)
```
The relationship between waste site counts and asthma prevalence is statistically signficant. 

```{r}
# Cancer
summary(model_cancer)
```
The relationship between waste site counts and cancer prevalence is statistically significant. 

```{r}
summary(model_copd)
```
The relationship between waste site counts and COPD prevalence is statistically significant. 

**summary**
Waste site counts are positively and significantly associated with asthma and COPD prevalence, with the strongest relationship being observed for COPD. The cancer model produces a small negative coefficient for waste sites. 


# Conclusion 
Despite the regressions showing positive and significant associations between waste site counts and the health indicators asthma and COPD, it is difficult to draw strong conclusions from this analysis for a few reasons. 

One issue is that some waste facility records appear to be stacked on the same coordinates rather than representing unique geographic locations. In some cases, multiple sites share identical coordinates, which suggests the points may be placeholders instead of exact facility locations. Because of time constraints, I was not able to fully investigate every site to confirm whether the coordinates reflect the true location of each facility. This means that the number of waste sites assigned to some census tracts may not perfectly represent the actual distribution of facilities.


Another possible confounding factor is the presence of other environmental hazards that were not included in this analysis. Waste facilities are not the only potential sources of environmental exposure. Some of these areas may also be located near other types of industrial sites, such as refineries or other facilities that produce pollution. If that is the case, it becomes difficult to determine whether the patterns observed in the data are related specifically to waste sites or to broader environmental conditions in those areas. It would have been great to run regressions that controlled for the presence of other types of industrial sites. However, time constaints did not make such regressions possiible. 

There were also limitations related to available health data. While the CDC PLACES dataset provides several tract-level health indicators, many potentially relevant outcomes were not available at the same scale. For example, I was interested in exploring birth outcomes, since they are often used in environmental health research, but I was not able to include this data due to spatial or temporal incompatibilities between datasets.

Because of these limitations, I am not fully confident in the strength of the relationships shown in this analysis. However, the results are still useful for exploring possible spatial patterns between waste facility locations and health outcomes. The analysis helped highlight areas where environmental facilities and certain health indicators appear to overlap.
Overall, this project raises questions that could be explored further with more precise facility location data and additional health indicators. In particular, incorporating birth outcome data and accounting for other nearby industrial facilities could provide a better understanding of how environmental exposures may affect community health.
